r: LAS 2810 asks students to synthesize primary works across visual art, literature, music, drama, and philosophy from antiquity through the Renaissance and to produce written and project-based interpretations of recurring humanistic themes such as origin, self-knowledge, and identity. Generating comparative essays or thematic summaries sits in the more-exposed band: task-exposure research finds writing and synthesis tasks strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and observed-usage data shows writing and office-adjacent tasks already form a prominent share of consumer and API use. The interpretive core connecting works across cultures and eras to shared thematic concerns is less mechanical than pure summarization, but AI tools already draft competent comparative humanities essays. With no general-studies designation to anchor an institutional floor, the rating tracks task content directly. The mandated three-event cultural attendance supplies only a modest, non-binding embodied component. At 24 months, adoption in undergraduate humanities coursework remains uneven, keeping the instrumental need only partially eroded.

By 2031, generative models will plausibly produce fluent thematic syntheses spanning the ancient, medieval, and Renaissance humanities canon on demand, and capability-trend data showing task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months suggests multi-source comparative writing projects of this scope fall well inside the achievable range. Verification burden here is moderate rather than severe: a misread thematic resonance in a Renaissance text is a quality problem, not the adversarial, high-cost failure that characterizes clinical or legal error, so expert oversight is not strictly required for every use. Because the general-studies designation field is empty, no gtPathways-style transfer mandate locks the course into a protected curricular slot, and the course is prerequisite substrate for only the single downstream course in its own two-part sequence. Absent both an institutional floor and a demanding verification requirement, the instrumental case for a student personally producing this interpretive synthesis work erodes substantially, even as encountering the material firsthand retains independent value outside this rating's scope.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems handling cross-period thematic synthesis, comparative essay drafting, and guided commentary on visual, musical, and dramatic works with high fluency; diffusion research (Census BTOS) suggests such tools will be broadly available in educational settings well before 2036, even granting that institutional adoption typically lags raw capability. The course's binding constraints remain thin: verification burden is moderate, embodiment is limited to occasional cultural-event attendance, and critically, the empty general-studies designation means no gtPathways or accreditation floor holds the course in place regardless of how automatable its tasks become. Its only scaffolding role is feeding directly into LAS 2820. The honest hedge is that ten-year projections for open-ended humanistic interpretation carry real uncertainty, and a course redesigned around live discussion and event-based reflection could partially offset the erosion. On the tasks as described, though, the instrumental case is substantially weakened.
LAS 2810.d: This interdisciplinary course, the first in a two-part sequence, is an integrated study of the visual arts, literature, music, drama, and philosophy of the ancient, medieval, and Renaissance world. It explores humankind's cultural legacy and focuses thematically on the concerns of origin, self-knowledge, identity, world-view and society that many cultures, both Western and Eastern, share in common and also takes note of the unique contributions of different artists, writers, and thinkers to that process. Learning approaches will include lecture, discussion, projects, and attendance at a minimum of three cultural events.

As with the first course, writing and thematic-synthesis tasks are strongly exposed: task-exposure research classifies writing and interpretive-summary work as positively associated with AI capability, and observed-usage data shows humanities-adjacent writing tasks are already common in consumer use. AI tools can already draft plausible essays connecting Romanticism, industrialization, and modern art movements. Verification burden is moderate, since a shallow reading of period context is a quality problem rather than a high-stakes error, and the mandated cultural-event attendance supplies only a thin embodied component. With no general-studies designation providing an institutional floor, the rating follows task content, partially eroded at 24 months given still-uneven classroom adoption of these tools.

By 2031, models will plausibly synthesize the modern humanities canon fluently, connecting Romantic, industrial-age, and twentieth-century developments across art forms and cultures, the kind of multi-source comparative writing capability-trend data on rapid task-horizon doubling suggests will be well within reach. Verification demands remain moderate rather than severe, so expert oversight is not strictly required for every instance of this work, unlike domains with adversarial or safety-critical failure modes. LAS 2820 is the terminal course in its two-course sequence, so it carries no further prerequisite weight for downstream coursework, and its empty general-studies designation field means no gtPathways-style mandate anchors it in a protected transfer core. Absent both a foundational and an institutional floor, the instrumental case for students personally producing this interpretive and comparative writing substantially weakens, even though studying the material for cultural literacy retains independent value the rating framework does not address.

The genuine hedge is uncertainty about how open-ended interpretation of cultural and historical meaning, rather than mechanical synthesis, will be valued and assessed a decade from now, and about whether the department redesigns the course around live discussion and event-based engagement to preserve an irreducibly human component. LAS 2820.d: As part of a two-semester sequence, this interdisciplinary course continues the integrated study of the arts and humanities in the world of the 17th through 20th centuries, from the baroque and the age of reason to Romanticism and the modern period. It considers the effects of scientific discovery, industrialization, social change, and technology on their development and the interaction of diverse cultures on an international and global basis, and also takes into account the unique contributions of different artists, writers, and thinkers.
